findings.topic: 1. Long voyages: why some players love the travel and others call it a snooze (ETS2 and Sailwind against Sunless Sea, Wind Waker and Sea of Thieves)
findings.works: Long travel is loved when three things are true: the hands have a light job, the ears have company, and the trip has a purpose. ETS2 players: "let your mind sink into the rhythm of the road and the mechanics until it all becomes almost automatic", "put on your favorite music or podcast", "working towards upgrades gives you a reason to keep taking jobs", "suddenly hours have passed". Sailwind players: "tranquil and meditative, with occasional periods of stress", "open seas navigation without a minimap, very satisfying". Both games keep the player doing something all the time (lane-keeping; trimming, tacking, taking star sights).
findings.fails: When the player only watches, slow travel becomes the top complaint. Sunless Sea: "minutes staring at a tiny boat crawling across a pitch-black screen", "waste hours upon hours on traversal and nothing happens during traversal", "glorified interactive loading screens". Sea of Thieves: "5 to 15 minutes" between places, "a walking simulator at this stage". Wind Waker: GameSpot said that by the last third "the focus on sailing ... is pretty tedious", and Edge found "an awful lot of relatively dull seafaring activity".
findings.kapman: This is Kapman's biggest risk. You decided on no steering (orders and "make for there"), so the voyage can slide into Sunless Sea's "watching a boat crawl". Keep that decision, but give optional hands-on jobs at sea that never stop: sail trim and reefing, rowing cadence, bailing, sounding, a lookout sweep, a fishing line, fixing your position by land and sun. Treat crew talk, sung work and the reading as the radio, the thing that keeps you company. Give every voyage a buyer and a date so it has a purpose. The rule in playability_and_fun.md of no gap over 4 minutes is right for stretches with no job. With a job and that audio company, longer quiet stretches become the ETS2 calm and not dead time. The 4x should be one key and work everywhere it is allowed.
findings.sources: https://store.steampowered.com/appreviews/227300 (ETS2 positive reviews); https://store.steampowered.com/appreviews/1764530 (Sailwind, both sides); https://store.steampowered.com/appreviews/304650 (Sunless Sea negative); https://store.steampowered.com/appreviews/1172620 (Sea of Thieves negative); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Legend_of_Zelda:_The_Wind_Waker

findings.topic: 2. Euro Truck Simulator 2: the relaxing-job formula, and how close Kapman's numbers already are
findings.works: Over 22 million sold by January 2026, PC Gamer's Sim of the Year 2012, called "unexpectedly engrossing", meditative and relaxing. The map is shrunk 1:19 (the UK 1:15) and a typical job runs about 20-60 real minutes (from memory). The loop is: take a job (a cargo, a destination, a deadline), drive, get paid, buy trucks and garages, hire drivers. Players praise "No shooting, no rush, no sweat", sunsets and rainstorms, and the community radio (TruckersFM) and multiplayer that grew out of mods.
findings.fails: Critics' complaints are mild (Metacritic 79). The calm depends on low stakes: a crash costs money and never ends the game. People who don't care for driving bounce off it, so it is a self-selecting audience.
findings.kapman: Kapman's numbers are already ETS2's: 1:40 against 1:19, Dorestad to London in 30-90 minutes against a 20-60 minute job. So pitch and build the ordinary voyage as "ETS2 at sea in 793". (1) Every voyage is a contract with a buyer and a date. (2) Ordinary trouble costs silver, time or standing, never the game; keep the wreck as game over for the recorded storms and plain carelessness, as storms.md already says. (3) Make the light and weather the show: dawn landfalls, rain squalls, fog. (4) Give a business ladder that buys a reason to take the next job: a bigger hull, a second boat under a trusted skipper, a storehouse at Dorestad.

findings.topic: 3. Friction and wind: what really made sailing tedious (Wind Waker HD, Valheim)
findings.works: Wind as a force you read and use is praised in every sailing game here: Sailwind's tacking and reefing, Sea of Thieves' sail angle, Valheim's karve and longship. Wind Waker's sea was "convincingly organic" (Edge).
findings.fails: Wind Waker's tedium had two concrete causes. One was the late Triforce fetch-quest across the sea. The other was the repeated wind-changing chore: IGN called it "a tedious nuisance", made worse by "the inability to skip the accompanying animation". Nintendo's HD remake added the Swift Sail (faster sailing, the wind always behind you) and cut the Triforce quest down. Valheim's "the wind is always against you" became a meme, fixed late in the game by a boss power that turns the wind (from memory). Sailwind complaints: a boat "stuck to the dock" when the wind is dead ahead, and "oars don't do anything".
findings.kapman: Keep real wind and Ohthere-style waiting for it, but: (a) every sail order is one key and acts at once, with no animation the player has to sit through; (b) never make late-game filler voyages across known water; (c) give a real counterplay to a foul wind: oars that actually make way, warping out on a line, riding the ebb out, or "wait for wind" as a choice that leaves port play to do; (d) let the auto-docking of "make for there" take over the last 50 m, because docking against the wind is the Sailwind pain point; (e) progression can buy better upwind ability (a deeper keel, a better sail), which echoes Valheim's earned wind control.
findings.sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Legend_of_Zelda:_The_Wind_Waker; https://store.steampowered.com/appreviews/1764530 (negative reviews); Valheim wind power from memory (not re-checked)

findings.topic: 4. Sunless Sea: slow ships, great writing, and the money and death spiral
findings.works: The writing won the praise: a Eurogamer 10/10, RPS's best game writing of 2014, IGN: "a wonderful world to explore that's packed with memorable written vignettes". Slow movement plus the music "creates an atmosphere of tension". A legacy (a will, a successor) softens permadeath. It sold 350,000 by 2018. Sunless Skies (Metacritic 87) was praised for "tales to tell, even when you fail miserably".
findings.fails: Steam negatives: "you never have enough money. Fuel and food are expensive", "constantly broke just trying to maintain basic supplies", "progress is constantly wiped out", "reading the same things multiple times, or... skipping past it", "no record of how you failed". GameSpot (6/10): it "falls well short" of the thrill of discovery. Sunless Skies drew GameSpot's "repetitive early storylines". Discovery runs out; upkeep grinds.
findings.kapman: (1) Food, water and pay must never eat the margin of an ordinary run. Upkeep should be a small, felt cost, not a treadmill that keeps a beginner broke. (2) Text encounters must track what the player has seen and never show the same text twice in a life. Repeats are the top complaint about text. (3) Keep a ship's log or voyage report that says what went wrong after a loss or a bad trade ("no record of how you failed"). (4) Heirs plus save any time already answer "progress wiped out". Show the heir inheriting something concrete: the boat's name, a debt, a feud, a map note. (5) Trade and the chronicle run on forever, so they are the right engine. Discovery alone runs dry, as it did for Sunless.

findings.topic: 5. Dredge: short trips, the hold as a puzzle, the night as a natural timer
findings.works: Over 1 million sold by October 2023, nominated at the BAFTAs and The Game Awards, Metacritic 80-85. It comes from a small New Zealand team (Black Salt Games). The loop is: a short trip out by day, fish, pack a Tetris-style hold, come back to sell and upgrade. Night brings a panic meter and danger. Players: "the cargo system is intuitive, fishing feels rewarding, upgrading is always tangibly beneficial"; "you can play this almost as a cozy game... no reason to take more risk than you'd enjoy taking"; "time only passes when you actually do stuff, not while sorting inventory"; "doesn't overstay its welcome" at about 12 hours.
findings.fails: "The gameplay barely evolves... the way you fish a simple Mackerel at the start is the same as... a rare exotic fish". Fetch quests. Some critics said the day/night cycle ran too fast and late progression was out of balance. Players wanted the night scarier, and one complained about having no minimap.
findings.kapman: (1) Make the Gislinge's 0.9 t hold a stowage puzzle: what to carry, where, the trim and the freeboard. Then every voyage starts with an interesting choice on the dock. (2) Spend the first hours on short Dredge-length hops (Dorestad to Traiectum and back, up and down the Rhine) before the first crossing. (3) Night and fog as optional risk with reward, never forced. (4) Freeze the clock while the player is in the ledger, the market or the stowage screen, or charge a fixed time per action, so the real-time clock never punishes reading. (5) A bigger ship must change how you play (crew council, more cargo kinds, open-sea crossings), not only the numbers, or Dredge's "barely evolves" will hit Kapman too.

findings.topic: 6. Sea of Thieves: the sailing feel keeps players; an empty sea lost them at launch, and authored riddles and visible world events won them back
findings.works: Physical sailing with jobs to split (sails, wheel, bailing, patching, the map table) and the stories that come out of it. 40 million players by April 2024. After launch Rare added Tall Tales, story missions with riddles called "brain teasers that really challenge player detective skills". It added world events marked by a sign in the sky you can see from far off, plus new factions and Adventures, and IGN told players to give it "a second chance".
findings.fails: At launch, content was thin and "players would not be motivated to complete quests because only cosmetic items are unlocked" (Game Informer). Steam today: "fun for the first few hours and then you keep doing the same stuff over and over", "can't keep loot in a game about pirates, what's the point?", 5-15 minute dead travel. Solo players are punished: Safer Seas cuts gold by 70%.
findings.kapman: (1) Your plan for hard written riddles is backed by the evidence: Tall Tales riddles are what fixed SoT's purpose problem. (2) Add signs visible from afar that pull the player off a straight line: smoke from a raided settlement, a fleet's sails, beacon fires, birds over a shoal, a wreck's mast. Each one is a beat the world makes, so it fits the rule of no timers aboard. (3) Rewards must change the game (access, standing, crew, routes), never be cosmetic only. (4) Loss of cargo hurts. Let insurance-like period practice (partnerships, shared ventures, a wife or partner holding the silver ashore) cushion it.

findings.topic: 7. Skull and Bones (2024): what an empty, grind-gated sailing game looks like
findings.works: Critics did like the ship-to-ship combat and the visuals.
findings.fails: Metacritic 58-63. GamesRadar+: "too much of a grind for too little reward". GameSpot: "Dead in the Water". No boarding or on-foot play. A world that feels lifeless. A silver-and-manufacturing grind economy with live-service currencies. Ships have a stamina bar that limits sailing. UK physical launch sales were less than a quarter of Sea of Thieves' 2018 launch, with about 850,000 players including a free trial, and the reported $200 million budget not expected to break even.
findings.kapman: This is the negative template. (1) Never put an artificial limiter on moving the ship. Only real limits: wind, tide, the men's tiredness at the oars, food. (2) The human layer is what fills the world: people in ports, crew, the council, text encounters. Plans that keep ports and crew "for later" risk a Skull and Bones first impression in play-tests. (3) Do not gate progress behind gather-and-craft grinds. Silver comes from trade decisions, not repeating actions.

findings.topic: 8. Trade economies (Patrician, Port Royale 4, Uncharted Waters, Bannerlord, Sailwind): what keeps buy-low-sell-high alive
findings.works: Patrician's 8 ranks, Shopkeeper up to Alderman, give a long, readable goal, and towns grow or decline with supply ("Micromanagement Heaven in 14th Century Europe", Computer Games Magazine). Uncharted Waters adds discovery reports to guilds for fame, supplies with scurvy and mutiny (from memory), translators and generations, which earn a long cult following. Sailwind players like starting with "an area-specific small boat... building your sailing skill, rep and wealth".
findings.fails: Patrician III scored 72-75, with repetition and unclear goals; the late game turns into automated spreadsheets (common player view, from memory). Port Royale 4 Steam: "unnecessarily convoluted and it tries to pack in too much content", "By the time I was ready to play, I couldn't remember half of what they showed me". Bannerlord: "workshops make nothing, caravans make nothing", "the trading and skill trees are meaningless". Sailwind: "prices change so much... bulk trading is nigh unprofitable", plus a request for "a JOURNAL? WE CAN WRITE ON?". Uncharted Waters: early reviews called it "an acquired taste" for its money management.
findings.kapman: (1) Keep trade personal and about information: one ship, prices you only know as of when news last reached you, news that travels by ship. This is a strength none of the spreadsheet games have. (2) Give a Patrician-style ladder of named ranks that change who deals with you. (3) Make the price response to your selling visible before you sell, so a dumped cargo is a choice, not a surprise (Sailwind's complaint). (4) The player's own ledger and notes on the chart answer Sailwind's "journal we can write on" directly. Make it prominent. (5) Passive income (a second boat, a storehouse) must matter but stay below your own voyages, and ask for a trusted man (Bannerlord's "make nothing" is the failure). (6) Uncharted Waters-style discoveries (a new landmark, a river mouth, a people) reported to a patron, a monastery or a king's reeve give standing: another endless engine beside trade. (7) Teach the market by doing it, not by front-loaded tutorials (Port Royale 4).

findings.topic: 9. Sid Meier's Pirates!: a career with an end, varied short activities, travel kept quick
findings.works: Over 1.5 million sold, Metacritic 88 on PC, "the year's most purely entertaining single-player game" (Computer Gaming World), praised for "solid gameplay design that combines a large variety of activities". The loop is sail, then a short self-contained activity (battle, duel, dance, trade, treasure map), then back to sea. A long personal goal (find the lost family). Aging slowly wears down your skills until you retire, and the game then ranks the life you led (from memory).
findings.fails: IGN: "the repetitive nature of the gameplay over time, and some mechanics that feel inconsequential". The minigames (dancing especially) wear thin once they are mastered.
findings.kapman: (1) Each life should end with a retirement scene: a chronicle entry that ranks the life (wealth, standing, places reached, people kept), then the heir takes over (CK3). That gives each generation a finish line and is a great hook for replays. (2) A personal long goal per life, written by you (e.g. a lost brother taken in a raid, a debt to clear, a vow to reach Kiev). (3) The port activities should be short and varied, but each must change something lasting. A minigame that doesn't change anything goes stale.

findings.topic: 10. Crew, council and characters (CK3, Mount & Blade, Saltsea Chronicles)
findings.works: CK3 (4 million sold by April 2025, an IGN 10/10) is praised for stories that come from traits and stress (acting against your nature costs you), councils and dynasty. Warband's companions argue with each other and leave when unhappy: memorable from very little text (from memory). Saltsea Chronicles (2023, Metacritic 78-84) has you choose a lead and a second for each landing; critics praised the "real and relatable" characters and its "issues" system for crew disagreements.
findings.fails: CK3: "when the story engine isn't firing, your actions can feel rote" (GameSpot); Steam: "the core loop is clicking through endless nested menus", "characters... aren't properly rooted in persistent relationships", "Everything exists separately, waiting for RNG". Bannerlord companions are generic and its sandbox "dull without mods". Saltsea: "too slow and tiresome... a lot of reading" (Gamereactor); RPS found it closer to a visual novel than an adventure game.
findings.kapman: (1) A small crew (4 on the Gislinge) means each man must be persistent and remembered: who argued, who was right, who saved whom. Relationships are the content. (2) Council decisions should be few and big. Show who agrees, and why, from their traits. Overruling a man's nature or faith costs his heart (CK3 stress). (3) Use Warband-style bickering and leaving: cheap to write, strong. (4) "Who goes ashore with you" (Saltsea) is a natural use of crew stats, culture and language in each port. (5) For the reading: keep each sitting short, only when pressure is low, and make the player's half active (pick the line, solve the kenning), or it becomes Saltsea's "a lot of reading". (6) Tie events to the people and the chronicle, not to random rolls (CK3's disconnected RNG complaint).

findings.topic: 11. Spectacle and a horizon worth watching (AC Black Flag, and its 2026 remake)
findings.works: Critics loved the naval side: The Escapist called it "a great dual system"; Edge praised the "much greater freedom by allowing them to explore, fight or sail whenever they wanted"; GameSpot said it was "every bit as important as running around on dry land". Seamless moves between ship and shore across 50+ places. Crew sea shanties, storms with rogue waves and waterspouts, and a horizon always full of sails and islands (from memory) made the sailing the part people remember. It was popular enough to get a remake (Black Flag Resynced, 9 July 2026).
findings.fails: Story missions were "repetitive and tiring", and the tailing and eavesdropping templates were criticized by GameSpot, Edge, Eurogamer, Game Informer and OXM.
findings.kapman: (1) Your crew singing at the oars is a proven pleasure. It has to be public-domain or CC0 recordings only (your rule), but it is worth hunting for. (2) Make storms rare, signposted set pieces, not a constant tax. (3) Make sure the horizon usually holds something: a sail, smoke, a landmark, birds. That is density without timers. (4) Keep the river-mouth prompt and the joins as seamless as you can. (5) Never fall back on mission templates (escort, tail, fetch). Encounters should come from the AI fleets and the chronicle.

findings.topic: 12. Authenticity as the hook, friction as the killer (Sailwind, Uncharted Waters, Dredge, Port Royale 4)
findings.works: Realism that is the fantasy itself gets praised by the people who come for it: Sailwind is about 88% positive on Steam with "No in game GPS, which adds deeply to the immersion" and "a real sense of accomplishment when you set out". Even its tutorials "sold as scrolls or manuals you can pick up" fit the world. Uncharted Waters' historical setting kept a long cult following.
findings.fails: Players punish friction that is not part of the fantasy: "The controls and UI for this game are nothing but tedious", "LEFT CLICK is used to drop items. Say goodbye to your fishing rod", a resolution bug, docking stuck in a headwind. Sailwind has been in Early Access since October 2021: "supposed to be out of early access by 2022", "no progress". "The world is dead... just static NPC vendors". Dredge players miss a minimap. Port Royale 4 has too much to learn at once. Uncharted Waters was "an acquired taste".
findings.kapman: (1) Keep realism where it is the dream: wind, tide, landmarks, real goods and prices, news that travels by ship, period trade practice. Cut or automate it where it is chores: mooring, stowage clicks, repeated orders, inventory accidents. (2) Without instruments, the chart must still help: your position grows uncertain offshore, but the last known fix and your own notes are always readable (Dredge's minimap complaint). (3) Ports must feel alive, with people, not vendor menus. Sailwind's "dead world" is its top complaint after bugs. (4) Stable first (your own rule): Sailwind's stalled Early Access shows that an endless build erodes goodwill. Ship a small, finished, polished slice (Dorestad, the Rhine, the crossing, Lundenwic) and grow from it. (5) Add an optional assist or difficulty setting for navigation and storms. It costs little and widens the audience beyond the sim purists.

summary:
The same lesson shows up in every game here: long, slow travel is loved when the player has a light job to do, company to listen to and a reason for the trip. It is hated when the player only watches.

**Where these findings come from.** The web-search budget for this session was already used up (200 of 200), so I couldn't run new searches. Everything comes from:
- the Steam review API, most-helpful reviews only (Sailwind, Sunless Sea, Dredge, ETS2, Sea of Thieves, Bannerlord, CK3, Port Royale 4);
- Wikipedia's reception and development sections (Sunless Sea and Skies, Dredge, Pirates! 2004, ETS2, Sea of Thieves, Skull and Bones, Wind Waker, Uncharted Waters, Patrician III, Warband, CK3, Black Flag, Saltsea Chronicles).

Each review fetch only showed a handful of reviews, so the quotes illustrate the complaints but are not statistics. Points marked "(from memory)" were not re-checked. I found no postmortem or GDC talk pages without search: the guessed Failbetter postmortem URL returned 404, and the Wikipedia pages fetched for Heaven's Vault and Sunless Skies held nothing on travel pacing or design changes. Recent indie coverage is thin too: Sailwind, Dredge and Saltsea Chronicles plus Skull and Bones. There is nothing on Sail Forth or other 2024-26 indies.

These findings extend section 1.8 of the existing design doc, G:\kapman_unity\Kapman2\Design\playability_and_fun.md, which already has a shorter comparison table. They do not repeat it.

**Who likes slow travel and who doesn't.** ETS2 (22M+ sold) and Sailwind (about 88% positive) turn slow travel into a calm the player enjoys. The player is always doing something (lane-keeping; trimming and star sights), has company (radio; the sea), and has a purpose (the job). Sunless Sea, Wind Waker and Sea of Thieves got their worst reviews for travel where you only watch: \"staring at a tiny boat crawling\", \"nothing happens during traversal\", 5-15 dead minutes.

**What that means for Kapman.**
- Kapman's numbers are already ETS2's: 1:40 against 1:19, a 30-90 minute crossing against a 20-60 minute job. Build the ordinary voyage as \"ETS2 at sea\": a contract with a buyer and a date, low stakes for ordinary trouble, the light and weather as the show, crew talk and song as the radio.
- The real risk is your no-steering decision. Keep it, but add optional jobs at sea that never stop: trim, reefing, rowing cadence, bailing, sounding, lookout, fixing your position.

**Other lessons, with the evidence behind each:**
- **Wind Waker:** the tedium came from repeated wind changes with an animation you couldn't skip, plus late fetch voyages. Make orders instant, never require filler back-and-forth trips, and give a real answer to a foul wind (oars that work, riding the ebb, waiting with things to do in port).
- **Sunless Sea:** its players were \"never enough money\" for fuel and food, saw the same text again, and had \"no record of how you failed\". Keep upkeep small, never show the same text twice in a life, and keep a ship's log that explains a loss.
- **Dredge** (1M+ sold): short early loops, the hold as a puzzle, and night as optional risk. \"Time only passes when you actually do stuff\" suggests freezing the clock in the market, ledger and stowage screens.
- **Sea of Thieves:** the purpose problem was fixed by riddle stories (Tall Tales) and events you can see from far off. That backs your hard riddles. Add smoke, sails, beacons and birds that pull you off course, and never give rewards that are only cosmetic.
- **Skull and Bones:** shows the failure case: an empty world, grind gates, and a stamina bar on the ship.
- **Trade games:** they go stale as spreadsheets (Patrician, Port Royale 4) and with passive income that \"makes nothing\" (Bannerlord). Kapman's personal, news-driven trade is its edge. Add a named rank ladder, show the price drop before you sell, report discoveries for standing (Uncharted Waters), and make the player's ledger and chart notes prominent. Sailwind players literally ask for \"a JOURNAL? WE CAN WRITE ON?\".
- **Pirates!:** end each life with a ranked retirement, then pass to the heir, and give each life a personal long goal.
- **CK3, Warband and Saltsea:** remembered relationships, bickering companions and \"who goes ashore\" carry the crew. Keep the reading short and active.
- **Black Flag:** sung work, rare set-piece storms and a busy horizon, never mission templates.
- **Sailwind:** realism only where it is the dream, automate the chores (docking, stowage clicks), make ports alive, and ship a small finished slice rather than an endless Early Access.

Twelve findings on game-design craft for Kapman, each with evidence and what it means for the game. How the research was done: the session had already used up its web-search budget, so I gathered evidence by fetching known pages directly (Wikipedia articles, Steam store pages and a Game Developer report of Sid Meier's GDC talk). I added well-known facts I did not re-check and marked each of those "(from memory)". Two sources could not be fetched: Soren Johnson's designer-notes.com was unreachable, and the Fandom wikis were behind a paywall.

The main points:
(1) Long travel feels calm, not tedious, when time is a resource and something small changes every few minutes. Euro Truck Simulator 2 (19:1 scale, over 22 million sold) and Dredge show this works; Elite Dangerous's "long, shallow valleys of boredom" and Sea of Thieves at launch show what fails.
(2) Kapman's travel tools are already the proven set: the auto-course, 1-4x speed, resting the night, and the date-jumping joins, which work like ETS2's ferries. The long-term risk is sailing the same routine routes over and over. The fix is to let the player hand routine runs to someone else (a hired skipper or a kinsman, like ETS2's hired drivers), not to add a time warp.
(3) A RimWorld-style director that paces events and offers player-chosen presets lets players set how busy the sea is without touching the clock.
(4) Trade becomes a spreadsheet when prices are fixed, information is perfect, or one loop is best. It stays fresh when price information ages and comes from sources of known reliability, when prices slide as you sell, when seasons and the chronicle open timed windows, and when contracts, contraband and debt add pressure.
(5) Crew stories come from a few visible traits, and changes in a crewman's state need to be announced loudly. Hidden layers of tangled simulation are noise to the player (Tynan Sylvester's "hairball"; Darkest Dungeon; CK3).
(6) With save-any-time, "wreck = game over" in practice means "reload". Sunless Skies offers both a lineage-of-captains mode and a reload mode. The same split could fit Kapman's heirs if the user wants it. Damage short of a wreck, and storms you can see coming, make storms produce stories.
(7) Keep history authentic where the player makes decisions and simple where it would be bookkeeping. Period words belong in the content, with a glossary, and plain words in the UI (Pentiment, Manor Lords, KCD).
(8) Give the reading rewards in parts (a Beowulf section per milestone, like Hades' story given out a little after each run). Let the player finish a reading by choosing from words they have learned. Check multi-part riddle answers in groups to stop guessing (Obra Dinn).
(9) Use the long first Dorestad stretch to teach, through the steersman, one system per stretch, and build the chart's notes like Outer Wilds' web of rumours.
(10) Every docking should pay something out and open overlapping goals over three time spans: the next leg, the season, and the life.

findings.topic: 1. Long travel: what makes it calm rather than tedious
findings.works: Euro Truck Simulator 2 compresses Europe to 19:1 (the UK to 1:15). It has sold over 22 million copies and won Steam's 2016 'Sit Back and Relax' award. Driving itself is a light task you never stop doing, and the scenery changes all the time. Dredge advances time only 'whenever the player performs actions such as sailing or fishing'. Days are calm; at night fog comes in and a panic meter rises. That makes time a resource, and it sold 1 million by October 2023. In Sunless Sea the slow ship creates 'tension' through fuel, supplies and terror; it sold 350,000 by 2018.
findings.fails: IGN on Elite Dangerous: 'brief, intense emotional peaks and long, shallow valleys of boredom'. PC Gamer: 'moments of emptiness, frustration, and boredom'. Sea of Thieves at launch: voyages were 'elaborated fetch quests' and the sea felt empty. It recovered only through content updates (40 million players by 2024). Death Stranding was called 'the most advanced walking simulator the world has ever seen', and reviews split. GameSpot faulted Sunless Skies for 'repetitive early storylines'. Tedium sets in on the 5th or 10th crossing of the same stretch, not the first.
findings.kapman: Kapman's 30-90 minute legs are ETS2-length trips, but they lack ETS2's hands-on driving because the ship follows the chart course with no steering. The calm has to come from two things. First, a sensory beat every 2-4 minutes in 3D: a landmark, a bird flock, a sail on the horizon, a change of light, the tide turning. Second, optional light seamanship: trim or reef in gusts, take soundings in shallows, bail, post a lookout. Make time cost something, as in Dredge and Sunless: stores, daylight, tide windows, and the end of the sailing season. A starting budget to test against: something to notice every 2-4 minutes, a small decision every 10-15, a real event every 30-45. Log 'minutes since last decision' in play-tests.

findings.topic: 2. Things to do while underway: the three modes as three levels of attention
findings.works: 80 Days combines travel, trading items between cities, and text encounters on the way into one loop. It has 750,000 words, of which a player sees about 2% per run, and it won the IGF Excellence in Narrative award. Outer Wilds' ship log keeps what you have learned 'organized either by location or in a web of connections', and learning is the only progression. Sea of Thieves turns sailing into tasks: sails, navigation, repair, bailing, the crow's nest. Dredge fills trips with fishing and fitting the hold. Assassin's Creed IV's crew sing shanties while sailing, and new shanties are collectibles (from memory).
findings.fails: Some reviewers found Dredge's fishing 'repetitive': the same chore again and again. Also failing (general pattern): mini-games that pull you out of the voyage, and text screens that hide the sea for long stretches.
findings.kapman: Design the three modes as three levels of attention on one running clock. The 3D voyage is for leaning back and taking it in. The 2D chart is for leaning in: riddles, notes, planning, the ledger. The isometric ship is social: crew talk, the council, reading aloud. The voyage keeps running at the chosen speed in every mode, and events pull you back (already decided). Size riddle work and readings to fit inside one 30-60 minute leg, so a leg feels like a chapter. Model the chart's notes on Outer Wilds' web of rumours: clues pinned automatically with their source, the player's own notes on top.
findings.sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/80_Days_(2014_video_game) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Wilds ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Thieves ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dredge_(video_game) ; Assassin's Creed IV shanties (from memory)

findings.topic: 3. Speed, autopilot and the fast-travel debate
findings.works: In Red Dead Redemption 2, holding the cinematic camera with a waypoint set makes the horse follow the road on its own; players use it as a relax mode (from memory). ETS2 has no free fast travel, but ferries and the Channel Tunnel are cut-overs at natural borders (from memory). It also lets you 'hire other drivers' to run jobs you don't want to drive (verified). Later Patrician games automate trade routes (from memory). In Elite, Hutton Orbital is a station with a very long supercruise trip to reach it. Players turned the trip into a pilgrimage with a mug as the reward (from memory). Length can be content when it is opt-in and marked as special.
findings.fails: Starfield was widely criticised because constant fast travel and loading screens broke the sense of one connected world (from memory). Elite makes routine work pass through long supercruise stretches. The opposite failure is forcing players to repeat traversal they have already seen in full, with no way to delegate it.
findings.kapman: Kapman already has the proven set: the auto-course, 1-4x speed, resting the night, and joins where the date jumps (the ETS2 ferry pattern). The user's rule of no time warp stands. The real tedium will come in hours 10-40, when routine legs repeat. Answer it with delegation, not warp: the merchant hires a skipper, or consigns goods with an AI trader or a kinsman, for routine runs. The world still runs in real time; the player chooses which voyages to live through. Two smaller ideas: on legs the crew know well, the steersman can take a known channel (knowledge shortens the trip, honestly). And speed auto-drops to 1x on an event, then returns to the player's chosen speed.
findings.sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_Truck_Simulator_2 (hired drivers) ; RDR2 cinematic camera, ETS2 ferries, Patrician route automation, Elite Hutton Orbital, Starfield fast-travel criticism (all from memory)

findings.topic: 4. Pacing events with a storyteller director
findings.works: RimWorld's storytellers pick events 'based on what it assesses will make the most interesting narrative'. Cassandra follows 'rising and falling tension', Phoebe allows 'additional downtime between events', and Randy 'forsakes a narrative altogether in favor of randomness'. Players choose one, which works as a difficulty and mood setting. In FTL a pursuing rebel fleet keeps you moving forward and stops grinding. Sid Meier (GDC 2012): 'Good decisions are situational'; 'It's almost worth erring on the side of providing the player with too much information'; 'The worst thing you can do is just move on.'
findings.fails: Pure randomness clumps events together and leaves long gaps. Repeated events wear thin (GameSpot on Sunless Skies' 'repetitive early storylines'). Choices whose stakes the player can't read feel arbitrary (Meier).
findings.kapman: Put a small director on top of the existing events and AI fleets. It tracks a tension value, which rises with risk (cargo value, contraband, raiding season, weather) and falls in port. It also tracks time since the last event. It draws from a deck of events tagged by place, season and date, with cooldowns and 'seen' flags. The chronicle supplies the big scheduled moments. Offer presets on the new-game screen: a Phoebe-like 'fair winds' for calm sailing and a Cassandra-like 'saga'. This lets players choose how busy the sea is without touching the clock. Every event choice should state its stakes in words, and every result should show a visible or audible consequence.

findings.topic: 5. Trade: information and rumours as goods
findings.works: In Sid Meier's Pirates!, tavern rumours decide where you sail. In Taipan!, 'a special price has occurred' messages on arrival create sudden openings. Sunless Skies sells a 'story-rich trading system' (Steam), and Sunless Sea lets you carry and sell port reports (from memory). In Patrician you see prices only where you have offices or ships (from memory), so knowing prices is itself an advantage. Sid Meier warns that choices made without information frustrate players.
findings.fails: Perfect information everywhere turns trade into a solved spreadsheet. No information at all turns it into blind guessing.
findings.kapman: Make information a good with an age and a source. Ledger entries show when the price was seen ('Lundenwic wool, 9 days old'). Rumours from met ships or taverns carry the teller's reliability, which could depend on crew traits or culture. News moves at ship speed, which is already built ('deeds' news travel'). Merchants carrying letters and news is period practice and a paid task: news of Lindisfarne, or letters for Alcuin's circle.
findings.sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sid_Meier%27s_Pirates! ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipan! ; https://store.steampowered.com/app/596970/ ; https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/gdc-2012-sid-meier-on-how-to-see-games-as-sets-of-interesting-decisions ; Sunless Sea port reports and Patrician offices (from memory)

findings.topic: 6. Trade: prices, risk, contracts, and stopping grind and exploits
findings.works: In Patrician II, towns decline when goods don't arrive, so supply and demand feel alive. Taipan! combines a risky high-margin good (opium 'confiscated at random... resulting in a fine'), debt with interest from Elder Brother Wu, and a clear goal: retire at £1 million. Sunless Skies offers 'Earn your fortune... or risk it all to become a smuggler' (Steam). Its ports post delivery requests ('Prospects') and discounted goods ('Bargains') (from memory). Meier: an interesting decision always involves a tradeoff.
findings.fails: Reviews call Elite's trading and grind 'repetitive'. Soren Johnson's rule is that 'given the opportunity, players will optimize the fun out of a game' (from memory; his site was unreachable). One dominant loop, fixed price tables, or buying and selling in the same port turns trade into a chore.
findings.kapman: (1) Prices slide with each unit sold and recover slowly, shown in the market panel, so the best route keeps changing. (2) Fairs, harvests, famines and raid years from the chronicle open timed windows of demand. (3) Commissions (already built) get a deadline and a named person, so each one is a destination and a small story. (4) Contraband law by realm plays the part of Taipan's opium: high margin, with the king's men searching. (5) The debt to the Frankish count plays the part of Elder Brother Wu: steady pressure. (6) Add a best-loop finder to the existing 10-year sim that flags any 2-3 port cycle above a set profit per hour, to catch exploits. Keep real goods and their real relative values, but tune absolute margins so a single leg makes a felt difference.
findings.sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrician_III (the page describes Patrician II) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipan! ; https://store.steampowered.com/app/596970/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elite_Dangerous ; https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/gdc-2012-sid-meier-on-how-to-see-games-as-sets-of-interesting-decisions ; Soren Johnson 'Water Finds a Crack' (from memory)

findings.topic: 7. Crew and characters that create stories
findings.works: Tynan Sylvester: 'The whole value of a game is in the mental model of itself it projects into the player's mind.' Players read stories into simple systems; RimWorld runs on traits, mood and mental breaks and has earned 'well over 100 million dollars'. Darkest Dungeon's stress leads to afflictions or virtues, and these 'were emphasized dramatically... using special graphics and sound cues'. It sold 2 million by 2017. In CK3, acting against a character's traits raises stress, and it had over 1 million sales in its first month. FTL's species each have one or two clear traits (Rockmen are fire-immune but slow).
findings.fails: Sylvester's 'hairball': with so many links between systems, players can no longer see cause and effect, and the stories get buried. Harsh rules added late feel unfair: Darkest Dungeon's corpses and heart attacks caused lasting player bitterness and were made optional.
findings.kapman: Give each crewman 2-3 traits, one want, one fear, and a faith and culture through which he reacts to events. Every trait needs at least one moment you can see: a line of dialogue or an action on the isometric ship. Add CK3-style unease: a Christian made to sail on a feast day, or a heathen made to pass a holy place without an offering, grows uneasy. At its peak, unease plays out as a loud scene: desertion in port, a fight, a vow. The council: 3-5 seats, each offering one option shaped by that man's traits. Keep pair relationships to a few named bonds (kin, friend, rival), shown only when they change. Tie personal wants to ports (a man wants to be home at Ribe for his sister's wedding) so they set route goals.

findings.topic: 8. Wreck as game over, softer failure, and saving
findings.works: In Sunless Sea, later captains 'inherit some of their predecessor's possessions', and the player can make a will. Sunless Skies offers 'build a lineage of captains as each dies, or reload your most recent captain and continue' (Steam), so players choose. In Pirates!, the hero ages and retires; the ending ranks you from 'beggar to King's advisor' by wealth, land, rank and marriage. FTL's permadeath works because runs are short and the team aimed for a roughly 10% win rate.
findings.fails: Kingdom Come: Deliverance's Saviour Schnapps saves: one outlet had logged '30 hours of real-time play, but only 19 hours' were spent moving forward, because of replays. A later patch added save-and-quit (from memory). Permadeath on top of long sessions means losing a whole evening, and that makes players quit.
findings.kapman: Current decisions: save any time, a wreck means game over and opens the load menu, and heirs come later (26 Sep: death passes to an heir; game over only with no heir). With save-any-time, a wreck in practice means a reload, so a storm is only as dangerous as the player chooses. Option for the user to decide, as in Sunless Skies: two modes on the new-game screen. 'Chronicle' is the current rules. 'Kin' saves only in port or by autosave; after a wreck an heir takes over with the family store, the chart and part of the standing. Add damage short of a wreck so storms produce stories: jettisoned cargo, a lost mast, running for a beach, a man overboard. Make storms readable hours ahead (sky, swell, warnings from met ships) so a wreck feels earned.

findings.topic: 9. Historical authenticity vs fun
findings.works: Pentiment keeps period scripts but adds 'a mode with easier-to-read typefaces', text-to-speech, and 'an extensive glossary of terms'. It consulted the manuscript scholar Christopher de Hamel and won a Peabody; the Guardian said its 'dialogue drips with fascinating historical detail'. Manor Lords' creator: 'in some cases considerations of gameplay superseded concerns of historical exactness'. It sold over 1 million on launch weekend and 3 million by February 2025. KCD sold its realism to over 10 million buyers. AC's Discovery Tour puts history in a separate combat-free mode of guided tours 'curated by historians', and Valhalla has a Viking Age one.
findings.fails: KCD's critics found the complexity alienating early and the save system contrived. Its claims about who lived in 15th-century Bohemia were challenged by academics. The Discovery Tour was 'heavily criticized' for historical liberties. Manor Lords was authentic but criticised for 'the lack of endgame challenge' and missing 'any kind of story'.
findings.kapman: Rule: be authentic where the player makes decisions (what sells where and when, seasons, tides, law, faith, who rules) and simple where it would be bookkeeping (weights, coin standards, exchange rates). Period words go in the content and plain words in the UI; this matches the user's verdict that period labels were 'obnoxious'. Use Pentiment's fix: hover any period term for a one-line meaning. Add a History side tab, separate from play like the Discovery Tour, with the sources behind each chronicle event. Keep saying plainly when something is a game tool (charts, the compass). Showing the real mix of 8th-century trade (Frisians, Franks, Saxons, Danes, Jewish traders, Arab silver) is both authentic and avoids KCD's representation fight.

findings.topic: 10. Reading and story rewards, and written puzzles
findings.works: Hades' story advances a little after every run and death. About 10 hours of dialogue make 'each attempt to escape meaningful'. 80 Days shows a player about 2% of its text per run, so each run reveals new writing. Return of the Obra Dinn confirms answers 'only in sets of three' to 'deter guesswork', and this 'became commonplace in the detective genre'. In Heaven's Vault you decipher an Ancient language of over 1,000 words from inscriptions, and guesses firm up as you see more (from memory). In Outer Wilds, learning is the only progression. In KCD, Henry starts unable to read and text stays scrambled until a scribe teaches him (from memory).
findings.fails: Walls of text handed out as a reward while the player wants to sail. Puzzles that can be brute-forced, or that fail for good after one wrong try. Answers that need outside knowledge with no way to learn it in the game.
findings.kapman: Hand out Beowulf in parts: the poem is divided into about 43 numbered sections called fitts, so one per milestone, read in the ship view while the voyage runs (a leg becomes a chapter). For 'the crewman reads part, you finish', make the finish a choice from words and runes you have learned (Heaven's Vault), not free typing. For multi-part riddles, check answers in groups as Obra Dinn does; this fits the user's rule that a riddle rests when tries run out and comes back once you learn something new. Audio: LibriVox says its recordings are public domain and has Gummere's Beowulf (from memory; check each recording). That fits the public-domain-only sound rule.
findings.sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hades_(video_game) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/80_Days_(2014_video_game) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_of_the_Obra_Dinn ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven%27s_Vault ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Wilds ; KCD reading skill and LibriVox (from memory)

findings.topic: 11. Onboarding a slow, complex game
findings.works: Dwarf Fortress on Steam kept all of its depth and added readable graphics (switchable back to the old ASCII). It sold 300,000 copies in the first week, and monthly revenue rose 'over 400-fold' from before. CK3 had 'the highest launch month sales for any Paradox Interactive title'; its tooltips that open into further tooltips and its tutorial are widely credited (from memory). Outer Wilds guides players with NPCs telling 'tales of distant lands' instead of quest markers. Meier: err toward giving too much information.
findings.fails: Critics found KCD's complexity alienating in the early hours. GameSpot faulted Sunless Skies' 'repetitive early storylines'. A long first session with no payoff loses players before the loop clicks.
findings.kapman: The 15-19 minute Dorestad stretch, which the user chose to keep long, is the stage for teaching. The steersman teaches one system per stretch, not through pop-ups: speed and the views, the chart, the ledger, waiting for the tide at the mouth, the lookout's call. Make the first voyage a commission with a sure modest profit, one event, and one riddle hook, all within about 45 minutes. Give every term and stat a tooltip that opens further tooltips. Start with a few known Frisian ports on the chart and the rest in fog.

findings.topic: 12. The 'one more voyage' hook and the shape of a session
findings.works: RimWorld playtesters 'couldn't bring themselves to leave until 2 AM', held by situations still unresolved. Pirates! and Taipan! give a long horizon: a retirement score, or £1 million. Hades gives a story payout every run. ETS2's job contracts break play into session-sized trips.
findings.fails: Manor Lords was criticised for missing endgame and story. In Elite, long dull stretches between the peaks. When every goal resolves at once, players stop.
findings.kapman: A 30-90 minute leg is the natural session. Each docking should pay out (a sale plus a story section or a crew moment) and open what comes next. Keep goals running over three time spans. The leg: a commission or a rumour. The season: a fair date, a crewman's wish, the end of the sailing season. The life: the family's standing, the heir, chronicle events you can see coming (Lindisfarne 793, the first raid on Dorestad in 834). End every port screen with 'what's pulling you next'. Close with a Pirates!-style family scorecard at death or at 1066.

summary:
The research points to one clear direction. Kapman's pitch (real speed, a compressed real map, trade, history, text encounters) has been proven in pieces. Euro Truck Simulator 2 sold 22M with a 1:19 map. Crusader Kings III sold 4M+ with start dates of 867 and 1066. Dredge sold 1M+ by building a tight 15-30 h boat loop region by region. Sunless Sea sold ~350k on its writing. The closest direct comparison, Sailwind (realistic sailing and trade), shows how small the pure-realism sailing niche is: ~2.4k reviews at 89%, SteamDB-style owner estimates of 50-100k, about 54 concurrent players, and still in early access five years after a launch target of Christmas 2021. Its negative reviews name exactly the gap Kapman plans to fill: "the world is dead... from one static NPC to another to deliver boxes", unprofitable trading, no manual save, no journal.

The three biggest risks are:
1. Dead minutes on long crossings. This is Sunless Sea's "tiny boat crawling across a pitch-black screen".
2. A confusing death and save rule. "Wreck = game over, but save any time" will turn storms into reload chores.
3. Scope. Kenshi took ~12 years, Banished 2 stalled on "code rot", Stonehearth and Spacebase DF-9 ended badly after early access, and Valve warns: "do not ask your customers to bet on the future".

What sells on Steam: a clear genre anchor, screenshots that show verbs and UI (users judge a game in about 4 seconds on hover), a trailer that shows gameplay in under 10 seconds, an early Coming Soon page, and a Next Fest demo. A demo's median playtime is the best early test. The median demo-to-wishlist rate is 19.3%, and a median under 24 minutes signals a problem.

Recommended vertical slice: Dorestad, the Rhine and the Frisian coast, plus one crossing to Lundenwic. That means 3-5 ports, the Gislinge only, a few goods, one season, a working storm, a handful of crew, 10-20 encounters, the chart with fog and one riddle, and one reading. Ship it first as a demo and then as a one-region game. Add the Baltic, Norway, the Rus river road and the North Atlantic later as region updates or DLC, the way ETS2 adds countries.

Limits of this research: this session's web-search budget was already used up, so the evidence comes from direct page fetches (Wikipedia, the Steam store and review JSON, SteamSpy, Valve partner docs, howtomarketagame.com, ESA 2025). Quantic Foundry blocked access, so there are no hard session-length figures for this genre. SteamSpy owner ranges are rough. Some review-JSON samples were small (Sunless Sea gave only 4 negative reviews in the sample), although their themes match the published critiques. Review playtime fields are in minutes and are not used.

findings.topic: 1. Who the audience is: older, PC-based, playing to relax, and spread across neighbouring genres more than 'sailing sim' fans
findings.works: ESA 2025 (US): 28% of players are 50 or older. Playing 'to pass the time or relax' is cited by 68% of Gen Z, 61% of Millennials, 63% of Gen X and 75% of Boomers/Silent. The Steam survey for Sept 2026 shows 95% Windows and 1080p at 48% (1440p at 27%). 8 GB and 16 GB VRAM are about equal (~27% each), and 32 GB RAM is most common (42%). The proven neighbouring audiences are large: ETS2 has 22M units and won Steam's 'Sit Back and Relax' award. Crusader Kings III has 4M+ and start dates of 867 and 1066, inside Kapman's era. Kingdom Come: Deliverance II passed 6M by June 2026. Manor Lords passed 3M by Feb 2025. Assassin's Creed Valhalla (Viking England and Norway) passed $1B.
findings.fails: The realistic-sailing niche on its own is small. Sailwind has 2,392 reviews (89%), SteamSpy estimates 50-100k owners, and it has about 54 concurrent players. Sailaway III has 102 English reviews and is Mixed (~70%). Sail Forth (cozy sailing) has 641 reviews (93%). Port Royale 4 (trade sim, launched at $39.99) has 2,149 reviews and is Mixed (57%). I found no reliable public data on session length for this niche (Quantic Foundry returned 403), and the Steam Deck share in the survey was not usable.
findings.kapman: Write for the Crusader Kings / ETS2 / Manor Lords player who wants to unwind, not only for sailing purists. The chronicle and the family line to 1066 are the hook for CK and history fans. The relaxing real-time voyage is the hook for ETS2 fans. HDRP must run well on 8 GB VRAM at 1080p, so keep a low preset. Without session data, assume evening sessions of roughly 30-90 minutes. Each one should be able to end in a port with a finished sale and an autosave.

findings.topic: 2. The closest comparison, Sailwind: players love realism but complain about a dead world
findings.works: Raw Lion Workshop's Sailwind entered early access in Oct 2021 at $19.99. It is rated Very Positive (2,121 of 2,392 reviews). It offers realistic sailing physics, navigation by compass and stars, cargo delivery, fishing, cooking, food and water management, and economies across three regions. Its top player tags are Sailing, Simulation, Open World, Survival, Immersive Sim and Relaxing.
findings.fails: It is still in early access five years later. The store page gave an 'optimistic' target of Christmas 2021 and a 'realistic' one of H1 2022, and reviews from the last 30 days drop to 78%. Negative reviews say: 'The world is dead...just going from one static NPC to another to deliver boxes'. They report a broken economy with unprofitable trading, no manual save, no journal and a clunky UI. One says: 'Critical issues from 2022 are still here...Dev is more worried about adding new sails'. Another: 'MASSIVE unrealistic waves that trap you for an eternity until you sink'.
findings.kapman: Kapman is essentially Sailwind plus real history plus a living world. What Sailwind players miss is exactly what Kapman plans: AI traders, raiders and king's men on lanes, text NPCs, reputation, and a chronicle that moves markets. Those systems are the selling point, so build them before more ships, ports or polish. A manual save, a journal (the chart notes) and a working trade margin are basic expectations.

findings.topic: 3. Slow travel, Sunless Sea's warning: watching a boat crawl is the top complaint
findings.works: Sunless Sea raised ~£100k on Kickstarter and has a Metacritic of 81 (Eurogamer 10/10). It won Rock, Paper, Shotgun's best writing award for 2014 and sold 350k by 2018. On Steam it has ~9.6k reviews at 83%. The writing and the mood carry it. 80 Days (Inkle) shows the other approach: travel by real geography is handled as route choices plus ~750,000 words of encounters, of which ~2% are seen per run. That is why people replay it. It scored 84-88 on Metacritic and won the IGF narrative award.
findings.fails: Sunless Sea negative reviews say 'The ship moves at a snail's pace', 'You spend minutes staring at a tiny boat crawling across a pitch-black screen' and 'You never have enough money. Fuel and food are expensive'. Others say it 'revolves entirely around you dying over and over' and call it a 'Wall of text with glorified interactive loading screens'. GameSpot gave it 6/10, saying it 'falls well short' of the thrill of discovery. Its sequel, Sunless Skies, was still criticised for 'repetitive early storylines' (GameSpot).
findings.kapman: Kapman has every Sunless Sea risk at once: a slow ship, supplies, a lethal wreck, heirs and text encounters. Since there will be no time warp, pacing has to come from what fills the minutes. In playtests, measure the longest stretch without a decision or a new sight. The map-side activities (riddles, notes), crew talk, readings, weather and lookout calls are core features, not extras. Make the first legs short river hops and hold the long open-sea crossings until those activities exist. Make supplies a decision taken in port, not a slow drain at sea. Write encounters so each run sees only a fraction of them, as 80 Days does, so they feel fresh.

findings.topic: 4. ETS2 proves that real speed on a compressed real map can sell, and its region-DLC model fits Kapman
findings.works: Euro Truck Simulator 2 renders Europe at 1:19 (the UK at 1:15) and is driven at real speed. It has sold over 22M units and ranked 5th among the highest-rated Steam games (April 2026). Critics praised how easy the GPS and map are, the option to stream real internet radio, the varied scenery and how 'unexpectedly engrossing' it is. It is still selling 14 years on, through free updates to old map areas plus paid country expansions.
findings.fails: Critics are lukewarm (Metacritic 79). The appeal is a mood, not reviewer excitement. There is a gap in the sources: the article gives no figure for ETS2's own time compression.
findings.kapman: This is the strongest evidence that Kapman's 1:40 world at real ship speed is sellable. Copy what supports the long drive: a clear route line on the chart, an audio companion (crew voices, readings and CC0 sea and bird sound in place of radio), and landmarks often enough that the view keeps changing. Copy the business model too: launch one region and sell the Baltic, Norway, the Rus river road and the North Atlantic as later region expansions. That turns the 240-port dream into a 10-year product plan instead of one huge launch.

findings.topic: 5. Tight scope and tension won for Dredge: polish one area, then add regions at a known cost
findings.works: Dredge comes from a small team (credited leads: producer, programmer/writer, artist, composer). It spent its 'first six months' refining the starting area, then 'each biome took roughly two to three months'. It sold 100k on day one, which the team expected to take a year, and 1M by Oct 2023. On Steam it has 57k reviews at 96%. Reviews praise a simple, satisfying loop, the atmosphere, a 10-30 h length ('They respect your time', 'Nothing i ever did felt like pointless busywork') and the cozy-versus-dread balance. Daytime is calm and 'inviting' and night brings the danger.
findings.fails: Critics called the fishing 'dull and repetitive', said the days were 'too short', and some players wished for more content.
findings.kapman: Dredge's process is the model to follow. At 2-3 months per region, Kapman's six or more regions are years of work, so the first release should be one region done to Dredge's standard. Kapman can use the same calm-and-danger rhythm: daytime river trading against night, fog, storms and raiders at sea. A finished 15-30 hour first campaign with an arc (for example, from a Dorestad boy to a known merchant by around 810) will review better than an endless sandbox at launch.

findings.topic: 6. Trade games die when money stops mattering: goals, endgame and economy feedback
findings.works: Sid Meier's Pirates! (2004) sold 1.5M. It mixes short activities (sailing, gunnery, fencing, dancing, sneaking) and ages the captain until his career ends, which drives replays. In Uncharted Waters, discoveries and trade earn fame that unlocks titles and opportunities, and it keeps a large cult following in East Asia. Sailing Era (2023), a modern game in the same style, has 441 English reviews at 83%. Crusader Kings III's emergent character stories won 91 on Metacritic.
findings.fails: Banished (solo, 5,500 hours, Metacritic 73) was criticised for 'lack of feedback for player actions', survival pressure that fades as towns grow, and no endgame goals. Manor Lords drew complaints about missing endgame challenge. In a sample of 100 recent negative reviews, about 15 complain about endgame tedium and about 10 about economy imbalance ('Importing goods is x10 the cost of exporting'). Sailwind players call its trading unprofitable. Port Royale 4 negatives cite 'unnecessarily convoluted' mechanics and too much micromanagement.
findings.kapman: Every sale needs visible feedback: the margin, the port's reputation change and the effect on the market. Goals must grow with wealth: a bigger ship, port privileges and charters, the family's standing, and chronicle shocks (raids on Dorestad, famine, Danish attacks) that break and remake markets. Pirates!-style aging fits the heirs-to-1066 plan, because each captain's career gets a beginning, a peak and an end. Keep trading quick to operate. Avoid Port Royale-style micromanagement.

findings.topic: 7. Wrecks, death and saving: 'game over, but save any time' sends a mixed message
findings.works: Death and succession can be part of a game's identity: Sunless Sea passes things on to a successor captain, Pirates! ends careers through aging, and Crusader Kings plays through heirs. Players accept loss when it is readable and the run continues.
findings.fails: Sunless Sea reviewers: 'The game revolves entirely around you dying over and over'. Sailwind reviewers complain about the missing manual save and about waves that 'trap you for an eternity until you sink'. When a loss feels unfair, players stop playing and leave negative reviews.
findings.kapman: With save-anywhere, most players will reload after a wreck. Storms then become reload chores, while players who forget to save lose hours. Option: make a wreck pass the family to the heir, with the ship and cargo lost and some reputation kept. The threat stays real, play continues, and the heir system becomes the death mechanic. An optional 'ironman' mode can serve purists. Storms must show warnings (sky, swell, crew advice) and be escapable (run for harbour, wait out the tide), never a trap.

findings.topic: 8. The first two hours: Steam's refund window and onboarding
findings.works: Steam refunds any game within 14 days of purchase and under 2 hours of play. For early access and pre-purchases, the 14 days start at release. Games that teach by doing keep players. Dredge's loop is called 'simple yet very satisfying' and 'easy-to-understand'.
findings.fails: Port Royale 4's negative reviews come after 14-133 minutes of play. They say the mechanics are 'unnecessarily convoluted' and that 'By the time I was ready to play, I couldn't remember half of what they' taught. Medieval Dynasty's mechanics were called 'poorly explained, making it especially difficult for newcomers'. Kenshi's UI 'can get cumbersome'. Manor Lords negatives say it 'doesn't explain a lot of things to you'.
findings.kapman: With 30-90 minute crossings, a new player may finish only one voyage inside the refund window. Script the first ~2 hours to deliver the core loop. The first river leg should be short and guided by a crewman (5-15 min). Then come the first profitable sale, a port arrival, a crew hire, a text encounter, a chart note, a weather change and a glimpse of danger such as a raider sail or a squall. Teach through crew dialogue in plain wording, not tutorial pages, which fits the user's preference for plain text.

findings.topic: 9. What sells: a clear genre anchor, screenshots that show verbs, an early store page and a demo
findings.works: Steam users judge a game in about 4 seconds on hover (four looping screenshots plus the top 5 tags). They often skip trailers and click through screenshots in 5-6 seconds looking for UI and verbs, and they read the negative reviews. Valve's advice: the first trailer should be gameplay, you may have under 10 seconds to make an impression, it may play muted, and put up a Coming Soon page as soon as you can. Wishlists trigger emails at launch and at discounts of 20% or more. Chris Zukowski (howtomarketagame.com): players buy by genre ('Because you played game A and B you will like C'), and art sells. Before the algorithm picks a game up, the median is 3,583 wishlists in 7 days and the minimum seen was 524. Demos convert a median of 19.3% of players to wishlists, and a demo median playtime under 24 minutes signals a problem. Manor Lords aimed for 14k wishlists, got 3M+, and sold 1M on its launch weekend.
findings.fails: 'Too unique' games with no genre anchor are hard to recommend. Mood text in place of verbs, a weak capsule image and an art-free page all hurt. Most demo players never wishlist, which is normal.
findings.kapman: Kapman combines a sailing sim, a trade sim, CK-style crew, text adventure and chart riddles. The store page has to anchor one line, for example 'Viking-age merchant sailing and trading sim'. Suggested tags: Sailing, Trading, Historical, Relaxing, Open World, Simulation, Exploration. Screenshots should show the ship under sail with the HUD, the trade screen with real goods, the foggy chart with notes, and a crew choice. The trailer should open on the ship at sea. The stylized look is a real visual hook, as Dredge's low-poly look was. For a Next Fest demo, use the Dorestad-to-coast slice (~45-60 min), ending on the first big sale or the first storm. Its median playtime is the cheapest test of whether the slow loop works.

findings.topic: 10. Positioning: 'chill with teeth', the Viking label, and authenticity players can see
findings.works: The 'cozy' label spread on Steam after 2020 ('only a handful' of games before, 'dozens' after) and reaches people who don't call themselves gamers. Dredge's mix of cozy and horror was praised. ETS2 shows that 'relaxing' sells. Viking settings sell: Valheim has 10M+, Assassin's Creed Valhalla (England and Norway, 872-878) had the series' biggest launch and $1B+, and Northgard is on 8 platforms. Historical authenticity is a stated selling point for Kingdom Come: Deliverance II (6M+) and was praised in Manor Lords.
findings.fails: 'Cozy' is vague and disputed. Viking hits sell on combat, raiding and survival, while Kapman's hero is a peaceful merchant. Wrecks, raiders and permadeath clash with a pure 'cozy' promise. Authenticity becomes a burden when it turns into homework (Sailwind's 'deliver boxes', Port Royale's micromanagement). Kingdom Come II's 'historically accurate' messaging also pulled the studio into culture-war fights.
findings.kapman: Market Kapman as calm voyages with real danger, the Dredge rhythm, not as 'cozy'. Put 'Viking Age' in the tagline for search and discovery, and frame the player as the merchant among raiders. That angle is fresh and fits the chronicle. Make authenticity visible in screenshots and on the store page (real port names, real goods and prices, dated chronicle entries, period ships) but never let it slow the loop. Keep the history in plain wording, which matches the user's own UI preference.

findings.topic: 11. Big worlds from tiny teams: they can succeed, but on a scale of decades, and early access punishes slowness
findings.works: Kenshi was made mostly by one developer over ~12 years, spent 5+ years in early access, sold 1M by 2020 and 3M by May 2026. Valheim, from a 5-person team, sold 5M in its first month and 10M by July 2022. It entered early access in Feb 2021 and reached full release in Sept 2026. Manor Lords, made solo, sold 3M+.
findings.fails: Stonehearth raised $751k on Kickstarter, spent 3 years in early access and ended without meeting its stretch goals. Double Fine stopped Spacebase DF-9 after early access, and fans were angry. The planned Banished sequel stalled from 'code rot'. Atlas, a sailing MMO with a world '1,200 times larger than in Ark', launched to exploits and server trouble. Sailwind has been in early access for five years. In Manor Lords' recent negative reviews (sample of 100), the top complaint (about 22) is slow early-access progress. Valve's guidance: 'Do not ask your customers to bet on the future of your game', and if you have 'a tech demo, but not much gameplay yet, then it's probably too early'.
findings.kapman: Selling a 240-port, 273-year world from day one is how Stonehearth and Sailwind ended up. Sell only what exists. Write the store page and any early-access promises around the one finished region. The project has already moved from Unreal to Unity, between URP and HDRP, and across four project folders (Kapman, Kapman2, KapmanLook, KapmanSail in G:\kapman_unity). Choose the stack and lock it after the sail tank and look test, because rebuilds are what killed Banished 2.

findings.topic: 12. The vertical slice and what to cut
findings.works: Dredge polished one area for six months, then added each biome in 2-3 months. ETS2 grew region by region over a decade. Zukowski's 'missing middle' advice: ship smaller games (1-9 months, $10-40k) as 'paid R&D' before the giant one. 'Sir, We Have an Orc Problem' (2 developers, 4+ months, 150k wishlists) took a proven hit and scaled one core element instead of mixing genres.
findings.fails: Kenshi's 12 years, Stonehearth's unmet stretch goals and Banished 2's stall show what happens when one huge vision is built all at once.
findings.kapman: Slice, one region in one season: Dorestad, the Rhine (Traiectum), the Frisian coast and one crossing to Lundenwic (optionally Quentovic). 3-5 ports, the Gislinge only, 4-6 real goods with working margins, one storm system done fully, 5-8 hireable crew with a simple two-way crew vote, 10-20 text encounters, the fog-of-war chart with notes and one riddle, one reading (a Beowulf passage), and chronicle entries for roughly 793-800. Defer: the Baltic, Norway, the Rus river road to Kiev, Iceland, Greenland and Vinland, bigger ships, the full CK-style council, the isometric crew mode (or a minimal version), the full 1066 span, Build mode, visual scripting and multiplayer. Add regions afterwards as updates or paid expansions, ETS2-style. Test the slice as a Next Fest demo before building the next region.
